symptoms: fast breathing (more than 60/min in infants, 50/min in 1-5 yr, 40/min in older children)
chest in-drawing (chest wall sinks during breathing)
guidance: Pneumonia is the single leading cause of child death under 5 in India. Seek emergency medical care immediately if fast breathing or chest in-drawing is present. Government hospitals provide free Amoxicillin or Cotrimoxazole for non-severe cases and injectable antibiotics for severe pneumonia. Do not rely on home remedies alone. Vaccination (PCV — Pneumococcal vaccine) prevents the most common cause.
precautions: Seek immediate medical care — do not wait and watch if fast breathing is present
Ensure child is vaccinated: BCG, PCV, Hib vaccines protect against pneumonia
Exclusively breastfeed for first 6 months — breast milk protects against lung infections
Avoid indoor smoke from wood stoves, incense, and tobacco near children
Count child's breathing rate for 1 full minute if cough or difficulty breathing is present

symptoms: loose watery stools 3 or more times a day
signs of dehydration: sunken eyes, dry mouth, no urine for 8 hours, crying without tears, skin pinch goes back slowly
guidance: Start ORS immediately — it saves lives. Prepare ORS: 1 liter clean water + 6 teaspoons sugar + 0.5 teaspoon salt. Give Zinc syrup (free at PHC) for 14 days — it reduces severity and prevents future episodes. Continue breastfeeding. Do NOT stop feeding child. Blood in stool (dysentery) needs antibiotics — see doctor. Signs of severe dehydration need hospital IV fluids urgently.
precautions: Start ORS from the very first loose stool — do not wait
Give Zinc supplements for 14 days (available free at Anganwadi and PHC)
Wash hands with soap before feeding child and after using toilet
Use only clean drinking water (boil if unsure)
Seek immediate care if child has sunken eyes, is not passing urine, cannot drink, or has blood in stool

symptoms: severe wasting — visible ribs, sharp collarbones, 'old man face'
guidance: SAM is a medical emergency. Refer to Nutrition Rehabilitation Center (NRC) at district hospital — admission is free under government schemes. NRC provides therapeutic feeding with F-75 and F-100 milks, then Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF — Plumpy'Nut). Treatment duration is 6-8 weeks. Community-based management with RUTF is now available. Growth monitoring at Anganwadi helps early detection.
precautions: Measure all children under 5 with MUAC tape — available at Anganwadi centers
Refer immediately to NRC if MUAC below 11.5 cm or edema present
Continue breastfeeding even in SAM children
Do not give high-protein foods rapidly — causes refeeding syndrome
Ensure complete vaccination and deworming as part of treatment

symptoms: appears shorter than peers of same age
often not apparent without measuring height
guidance: Stunting results from prolonged inadequate nutrition starting before birth. It causes permanent effects on brain development and height if not corrected before age 2 (the '1000 days window'). Interventions: exclusive breastfeeding till 6 months, diverse complementary feeding from 6 months (ragi, dal, eggs, green vegetables), IFA supplements, regular growth monitoring at Anganwadi. Prevention is far more effective than treatment.
precautions: Ensure mother's nutrition during pregnancy — stunting starts in womb
Exclusively breastfeed for 6 months — introduce diverse foods after
Take child monthly for weight and height measurement at Anganwadi
Ensure all 12 vaccines under Universal Immunization Programme
Deworm every 6 months from age 1 under National Deworming Day program

symptoms: yellowing of skin and eyes in newborn
appears within first 2-3 days of birth
yellow color spreading from face to chest and belly
guidance: Mild jaundice appearing on day 2-3 in healthy term babies is common (physiological jaundice) and often resolves by 1-2 weeks with frequent breastfeeding. Jaundice appearing in the first 24 hours, or spreading to the belly, or in premature babies is dangerous and needs immediate hospital treatment with phototherapy (blue light). Untreated severe jaundice causes brain damage (kernicterus).
precautions: Seek immediate medical care for jaundice in first 24 hours, or yellow belly, or poor feeding
Feed baby 8-12 times per day — frequent feeding helps clear bilirubin
Do NOT expose baby to direct sunlight — this can cause heat stroke and sunburn
Phototherapy at government hospitals is free
Report yellowing spreading below navel or baby becoming very sleepy as emergency

symptoms: sudden body shaking or stiffening with fever (usually 38°C or above)
occurs usually in children age 6 months to 5 years
guidance: Most febrile seizures are benign (simple febrile seizure) and stop within 5 minutes without treatment. Lay child on side to prevent choking. Do NOT put anything in the child's mouth. Time the seizure. Call 108 if seizure lasts more than 5 minutes or if child does not recover consciousness. After seizure, control fever and seek medical evaluation to rule out meningitis.
precautions: Lay child on their side during seizure — never put anything in the mouth
Do NOT restrain the child forcefully
Call 108 immediately if seizure lasts more than 5 minutes (status epilepticus)
Lower fever with paracetamol as directed by doctor
All children with first febrile seizure need medical evaluation to exclude meningitis

symptoms: ear pain (child may tug or pull at ear)
difficulty hearing or not responding to sounds
crying more than usual in infants
guidance: Most ear infections in children are caused by bacteria following a cold. Consult a doctor — bacterial infections require antibiotics. Apply warm (not hot) compress over the ear for pain relief. Do not put any drops, oil, or objects in the ear without doctor's advice. Recurrent ear infections or hearing loss need specialist (ENT) evaluation. A ruptured eardrum from untreated infection can cause permanent hearing loss.
precautions: Do not insert cotton swabs or any object into child's ear
Complete the full antibiotic course even if child seems better
Keep water out of ears during bathing — use cotton plugs gently
Breastfeed infants — significantly reduces ear infection risk
Seek ENT evaluation if child has had 3 or more ear infections in 6 months

symptoms: rash or blisters on palms, soles, and sometimes buttocks
drooling in young children due to mouth pain
guidance: HFMD is a common viral illness in children under 5. It is self-limiting and resolves in 7-10 days. Provide paracetamol for fever and pain. Encourage cool fluids and cold foods (ice cream, cold yogurt) to soothe mouth sores. Isolate child from school and other children while fever and blisters are present. Very rarely causes serious complications.
precautions: Isolate child until all blisters have dried and fever resolves
Wash hands frequently and thoroughly — virus spreads by contact
Disinfect toys and surfaces the child has touched
Do not squeeze or burst blisters
Seek care if child cannot swallow, has very high fever, or appears very unwell

symptoms: severe prolonged coughing fits ending in a 'whoop' sound
cough until child turns red or blue
in infants: may not whoop but may stop breathing during cough (apnea)
guidance: Most dangerous in infants under 6 months who can stop breathing during episodes. Seek emergency care for infants with suspected pertussis. Antibiotics (erythromycin or azithromycin) reduce contagiousness but do not stop cough once it has started. Hospitalization needed for severe cases. Recovery can take up to 3 months (hence called '100-day cough'). DPT vaccination prevents this disease — it is available free.
precautions: Vaccinate with DPT (Diphtheria-Pertussis-Tetanus) at 6, 10, and 14 weeks — it is free
Seek immediate care for any infant with coughing spells that stop breathing
Isolate child from infants and pregnant women
Complete antibiotic course — reduces spread even if cough continues
Pregnant women should get Tdap vaccine in third trimester to protect newborn

symptoms: soft skull bones in infants (delayed fontanelle closure)
enlarged wrists, ankles, and costochondral junctions (rachitic rosary)
guidance: Caused by Vitamin D deficiency, often combined with calcium deficiency. Treatment: Vitamin D supplements (Stoss therapy — high dose or daily doses) and calcium-rich foods. Expose child to morning sunlight daily (15-20 minutes). Vitamin D supplements (Navjaat Suraksha Kit) provided free at government facilities for newborns. Breastfed babies should receive Vitamin D drops from 2 weeks of age.
precautions: Expose child to morning sunlight daily — best between 7-9 AM
Give Vitamin D drops to all breastfed infants from 2 weeks (consult doctor for dose)
Include calcium-rich foods: milk, curd, ragi, sesame seeds (til)
Do not give excess Vitamin D without monitoring — causes toxicity
Consult doctor for any child with bowed legs or delayed walking

symptoms: no babbling or pointing by 12 months
loss of previously acquired language or social skills
does not respond to own name
over or under sensitivity to senses
guidance: ASD is a neurodevelopmental condition — not a disease or result of bad parenting. Early identification (ideally before age 3) and early intervention dramatically improve outcomes. Government programs under Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK) provide free screening and intervention. Therapies include Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA), speech therapy, occupational therapy, and special education. Vaccinations do NOT cause autism — this is a disproven myth.
precautions: Monitor developmental milestones at every well-child visit — use RBSK screening
Act early — do not 'wait and see' if development seems delayed
Vaccines do NOT cause autism — continue full vaccination schedule
Contact NIMH (National Institute of Mental Health) or district early intervention center
Connect with parent support groups — improves coping and outcomes for families

symptoms: delayed motor milestones (not sitting by 9 months, not walking by 18 months)
walking on toes or scissor gait
using only one side of the body
guidance: Cerebral palsy is caused by brain injury around birth (asphyxia, prematurity, infection). It is not progressive — the brain injury does not worsen, though its effects change as the child grows. Management includes physiotherapy, speech therapy, occupational therapy, and assistive devices. Free rehabilitation services available under Persons with Disabilities Act and RBSK. Early intervention before age 3 gives best outcomes.
precautions: Enroll child in early intervention program as early as possible
Physiotherapy should be consistent and started early
Prevent birth asphyxia — deliver in hospital with skilled birth attendants
Prevent prematurity — attend all ANC visits and manage risk factors
Apply for disability certificate — entitles child to free education and rehabilitation services

symptoms: sudden severe cramping abdominal pain (child pulls knees to chest and cries)
blood and mucus in stool (red currant jelly stool)
child becomes pale and lethargic between pain episodes
guidance: This is a surgical emergency where one part of the intestine folds into another, cutting off blood supply. Most common in children 6 months to 3 years. Seek emergency care immediately. Treatment is air or barium enema (non-surgical) in early cases or surgery in late or complicated cases. Do not give food or water — rush to hospital immediately.
precautions: Rush to hospital immediately — time is critical to prevent bowel death
Do not give food, water, or pain medicines — go directly to emergency
Do not apply heat pads or press the abdomen forcefully
Rotavirus vaccine reduces risk of intussusception after viral diarrhea
Early treatment (within 24 hours) avoids surgery in most cases

symptoms: preventable diseases include: TB, polio, diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus, hepatitis B, measles, rubella, Japanese Encephalitis, rotavirus diarrhea, pneumococcal pneumonia, typhoid
guidance: India's Universal Immunization Programme (UIP) provides all childhood vaccines FREE. Full schedule: BCG at birth, OPV + IPV + Pentavalent + PCV + Rotavirus at 6,10,14 weeks, MR/MMR at 9-12 months and 16-24 months, DPT booster at 16-24 months, JE vaccine at 9-12 months (in endemic areas), Typhoid vaccine at 9-12 months. Missing vaccines can be caught up — nearest PHC or Anganwadi can advise. Never miss a vaccination opportunity.
precautions: Carry the immunization card (Mamta card) to every visit — never lose it
Child can receive vaccines even with mild cold or fever — do not postpone
Mild fever or swelling at injection site is normal — do not panic
Seek care if child develops high fever (above 40°C) within 48 hours of vaccine
All vaccines are free — do NOT pay for them at government facilities

symptoms: unable to sit still, runs or climbs excessively
symptoms present in more than one setting (home and school)
guidance: ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition affecting 5-10% of school-age children. It is NOT caused by poor parenting, too much screen time, or sugar. Diagnosis requires a comprehensive evaluation by a pediatrician or child psychiatrist. Treatment combines behavior therapy, school accommodations, and in some cases medication. Children with ADHD have average to above-average intelligence and can succeed with right support.
precautions: Consult a pediatrician or child psychiatrist for proper diagnosis — do not self-diagnose
Work with school to provide academic accommodations
Structured routines, short tasks, and positive reinforcement help greatly
Screen time should be limited and structured
Do not use traditional 'scolding and beating' discipline — it worsens ADHD symptoms

guidance: This is a medical emergency. Hospitalize immediately — sepsis is the leading cause of neonatal mortality in India. IV antibiotics (ampicillin + gentamicin) must be started within 1 hour. Supportive care: IV fluids, oxygen, temperature regulation. Prevent through clean delivery practices and handwashing.
precautions: Deliver in a clean facility (institutional delivery)
Keep umbilical cord clean and dry
Do not apply traditional substances (ghee, oil) on cord
Seek care immediately if baby stops feeding or becomes lethargic

symptoms: yellowing of skin and eyes on day 2-3 of life
baby is alert and feeding well
stool is yellow or green, urine is pale
resolves by 10-14 days in term babies
guidance: Mild physiological jaundice is common and usually benign. Feed baby frequently (8-12 times/day) — good hydration helps clear bilirubin. Do not give water or sugar water — breast milk is best. No treatment needed for mild cases. If jaundice spreads to the belly or beyond, or if baby is lethargic, see a doctor.
precautions: Do not expose to direct sunlight (risk of sunburn)
Seek care if baby is not feeding well, is sleepy, or jaundice appears in first 24 hours
Know that phototherapy at government hospitals is free if needed

symptoms: jaundice appearing within first 24 hours of life
rapidly spreading to hands and feet
baby is lethargic, not feeding well, irritable, high-pitched cry
severe cases: kernicterus (brain damage) — arching of back, seizures, deafness
guidance: MEDICAL EMERGENCY — Hospitalization required. Treatment: phototherapy (blue light). Exchange transfusion for severe cases. Early detection prevents brain damage. Risk factors: prematurity, ABO/Rh incompatibility, G6PD deficiency.
precautions: Seek immediate care for jaundice in first 24 hours
Monitor for lethargy and poor feeding
Ensure all newborns are checked for jaundice before discharge
Rh-negative mothers should receive anti-D immunoglobulin
Follow up bilirubin levels as advised

symptoms: baby does not cry immediately after birth
pale or blue skin at birth
guidance: EMERGENCY — Requires immediate resuscitation at birth. Therapeutic hypothermia (cooling therapy) is proven to improve outcomes if started within 6 hours of birth. Prevention: good antenatal care, timely C-section for obstructed labor, skilled birth attendance.
precautions: Deliver in a hospital with skilled birth attendants
Monitor fetal heart rate during labor
Do not delay C-section if obstructed labor
Ensure newborn resuscitation equipment is available
All babies with birth asphyxia need neurological follow-up

category: Neonatal Hypoglycemia (Low Blood Sugar in Newborns)
guidance: At-risk babies (small for gestational age, large for gestational age, premature, maternal diabetes) need early and frequent feeding — breastfeed within 1 hour of birth. If blood sugar < 40 mg/dL, IV glucose is given in hospital. Prevention: early initiation of breastfeeding and avoiding delays.
precautions: Initiate breastfeeding within 1 hour of birth
Feed at-risk babies more frequently (every 2 hours)
Monitor blood sugar in high-risk babies
Do not give glucose water by mouth as a substitute for breast milk
Seek care if baby shows jitteriness or seizures

guidance: Warm the baby immediately using skin-to-skin contact (Kangaroo Mother Care). Keep room warm (25-28°C). Dry the baby thoroughly after birth. Delay the first bath for at least 24 hours. Hypothermia is a major risk for infection and death in newborns. Government facilities have warmers.
precautions: Cover baby's head with a cap
Delay bathing for 24 hours after birth
Use a warm blanket if needed

guidance: Premature babies are at highest risk due to surfactant deficiency. Treatment: antenatal steroids (given to mother before delivery if preterm birth is anticipated), surfactant replacement therapy, and respiratory support (CPAP or mechanical ventilation). This is managed in the NICU. Free care under government schemes.
precautions: Prevent preterm birth with good ANC
Deliver in a facility with NICU capability if preterm
Surfactant is life-saving and available in government hospitals

symptoms: respiratory distress in a term or post-term baby
baby is large for gestational age
guidance: Meconium in amniotic fluid indicates fetal distress. At delivery: if baby is not vigorous, suction the airway before stimulation. Treatment: oxygen, surfactant, inhaled nitric oxide, and mechanical ventilation. Prevent post-term pregnancy by induction if indicated.
precautions: Do not delay delivery if fetal distress is detected
Suctioning of the airway at birth for non-vigorous babies

symptoms: tachypnea (breathing > 60/min) starting within hours of birth
oxygen saturation normal or mildly low
guidance: TTNB is a self-limiting condition due to delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid. It is more common in babies born by C-section without labor. Supportive care: supplemental oxygen, CPAP if needed. No antibiotics unless sepsis cannot be ruled out. Prognosis is excellent.
precautions: Feeding can be started once breathing improves

symptoms: abdominal wall discoloration or redness (late sign)
guidance: NEC is a life-threatening bowel emergency in premature infants. Treatment: stop feeding, IV antibiotics, nasogastric decompression, IV fluids, and TPN. Surgery for perforation or intestinal necrosis. Prevention: exclusive breastfeeding (BM provides protective factors), probiotics, and standardized feeding protocols.
precautions: Exclusive breast milk feeding (fortified if needed)

symptoms: in severe cases: rapid deterioration, coma
guidance: IVH is common in premature infants due to fragile germinal matrix vessels. Diagnosis by cranial ultrasound. Mild IVH (grade I-II) often resolves. Severe IVH (grade III-IV) leads to hydrocephalus and cerebral palsy. Prevention: antenatal corticosteroids, maintaining stable BP, and avoiding rapid fluctuations.
precautions: Serial cranial ultrasounds for premature babies

guidance: ROP is a potentially preventable cause of childhood blindness. All babies < 34 weeks or < 1750g birth weight must be screened for ROP starting at 4-6 weeks of age, as per national guidelines. Treatment (laser or anti-VEGF) prevents blindness. Free screening in government NICU networks.
precautions: Strict oxygen monitoring in preterm infants
Awareness among parents of preterm babies

guidance: EMERGENCY — High mortality. Treatment: tetanus antitoxin, antibiotics (metronidazole), diazepam for muscle spasms, wound care (umbilical stump). Prevention is key: maternal TT vaccination and clean delivery practices. India has almost eliminated neonatal tetanus.
precautions: Ensure all pregnant women receive 2 doses of TT vaccine
Deliver in a clean health facility
Use sterile instruments to cut cord
Do not apply cow dung or other substances on cord

guidance: Prevent by screening all pregnant women for syphilis (free at PHCs). Treatment: Penicillin is curative in fetus if mother is treated early. Congenital syphilis is a notifiable disease. Early treatment prevents long-term neurological and bone damage.
precautions: Follow-up of infants born to treated mothers
Do not miss the VDRL/RPR test in pregnancy

guidance: HIV is transmitted from mother to child. Prevention: maternal ART during pregnancy and breastfeeding. All HIV-exposed infants must receive prophylactic ART (nevirapine or AZT) for 6 weeks. HIV testing (DNA PCR) at 4-6 weeks. Lifelong ART is available free at ART centers under NACO.
precautions: Exposed infants should receive prophylactic medications
Avoid mixed feeding (exclusive breastfeeding or exclusive formula)

guidance: CMV is the most common cause of congenital infection. Prevention: hand hygiene (avoid saliva from young children during pregnancy). Diagnosis by urine PCR in first 2 weeks. Antiviral (valganciclovir) improves hearing outcomes in symptomatic infants.
precautions: Pregnant women should avoid sharing utensils and foods with young children

guidance: Diagnosis: karyotype or FISH. Management: regular growth and developmental monitoring, cardiac evaluation, thyroid screening (annual), vision and hearing checkups. Early intervention (physiotherapy, speech therapy, special education) improves quality of life. Government facilities provide free care and support.
precautions: Cardiac evaluation in first few weeks

guidance: Diagnosis: karyotype. Growth hormone therapy can improve height. Estrogen replacement for puberty induction. Regular cardiac monitoring. Hearing and eye checkups. Most have normal intelligence but may have learning difficulties in math.

symptoms: facial cleft at birth (lip, palate, or both)
guidance: Early management: specialized feeding techniques (pigeon bottle, palatal obturator). Surgical repair: cleft lip at 3-6 months, palate at 9-18 months. Ongoing speech therapy, dental care, and audiology. Free surgeries under government schemes like Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK).

symptoms: foot is turned inward and downward
guidance: Treat with Ponseti method (serial casting and bracing) — it is highly effective (90% success). Start within first few weeks of life. Free treatment available under RBSK. Neglected clubfoot leads to permanent disability.
precautions: Do not attempt traditional manipulation (can cause fractures)

symptoms: click or clunk on Ortolani/Barlow tests
guidance: Screen all newborns with clinical hip examination. Ultrasound for high-risk (breech, family history). Treatment: Pavlik harness (if <6 months), closed or open reduction for older. Early detection prevents long-term hip arthritis and disability.

symptoms: urethral opening on the underside of the penis
guidance: Surgical correction (urethroplasty) is usually performed between 6-18 months of age. Do not circumcise before surgical repair (foreskin is used in surgery). Good outcomes with experienced pediatric surgeons.
precautions: Do not circumcise without consulting a pediatric surgeon
Do not delay surgery beyond 18 months for psychological reasons

category: Congenital Heart Defects (VSD, ASD, PDA, TOF)
guidance: Suspected heart defects need echocardiography. Treatment ranges from medical management (diuretics) to surgical repair or catheter intervention (coil occlusion, balloon valvuloplasty). Government hospitals provide free surgery under PMJAY and RBSK screening.
precautions: Antibiotic prophylaxis for infective endocarditis before procedures
Monitor for cyanosis and failure to thrive
Do not miss newborn pulse oximetry screening (critical CHD)

symptoms: crying for >3 hours per day, >3 days per week, for >3 weeks
crying episodes often in the evening
baby is otherwise healthy and gaining weight
guidance: Colic is self-limiting, usually resolving by 3-4 months. Soothe baby with gentle rocking, swaddling, white noise, and a warm bath. Burp baby well during and after feeds. Dietary changes (eliminate cow's milk if formula-fed) may help. Check for reflux or cow's milk protein allergy.
precautions: Hold baby upright for 30 min after feeds
Seek care if fever, poor weight gain, or bilious vomiting develops

guidance: Positional management (upright after feeds). Thickening feeds (with rice cereal). If severe, medication (antacids, H2 blockers, PPIs) under medical supervision. Most resolve by 12-18 months. Identify cow's milk protein allergy (CMPA) as a common cause.
precautions: Keep baby upright for 30 minutes after feeding
Do not put baby to sleep flat on back with reflux (but still back sleeping for SIDS prevention)
Consult a pediatrician for persistent symptoms

symptoms: progressive non-bilious projectile vomiting at 2-8 weeks of age
guidance: Surgical condition — requires pyloromyotomy. Correct dehydration and electrolytes (hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis) before surgery. Surgery is curative. Do not delay.
precautions: Seek immediate care for projectile vomiting in infants
Do not try home remedies for projectile vomiting

symptoms: red currant jelly stool (blood and mucus)
guidance: MEDICAL EMERGENCY. Early cases can be treated with air or barium enema (non-surgical). If diagnosed late, surgery is needed. Do not give anything by mouth. Time is critical to prevent bowel ischemia and perforation.
precautions: Do not give food or water
Rotavirus vaccine is associated with a slight risk — but benefits outweigh risks

symptoms: failure to pass meconium or delayed
guidance: EMERGENCY — Midgut volvulus leads to bowel necrosis within hours. Upper GI series or contrast enema for diagnosis. Emergency surgery (Ladd's procedure) is needed. Prognosis depends on time to diagnosis.
precautions: Any bilious vomiting in a newborn is a surgical emergency
Long-term follow-up for short gut if extensive resection

symptoms: failure to pass meconium within 48 hours of birth
guidance: Diagnosis: rectal biopsy (absence of ganglion cells). Surgical treatment: pull-through procedure (Swenson, Soave, Duhamel). Early surgery prevents enterocolitis. Stoma may be needed in sick babies.

Diagnosis: tissue transglutaminase IgA (ttg IgA), total IgA, and duodenal biopsy for confirmation. Treatment: strict lifelong gluten-free diet (avoid wheat, barley, rye). Follow-up: growth monitoring, bone density, and nutritional status.

symptoms: poor weight gain despite adequate intake
guidance: Investigate the cause: inadequate intake, malabsorption, increased losses, increased requirements, or psychosocial factors. Treatment: nutritional rehabilitation, feeding support, and addressing underlying medical or social issues. Regular follow-up in nutritional rehabilitation programs.
precautions: Ensure adequate caloric and protein intake

guidance: Treatment: oral iron supplements (3-6 mg/kg/day) for 3 months. Dietary sources: green leafy vegetables, jaggery, eggs, meat, fortified cereals. Iron supplementation is given to all children aged 6-60 months under the National Anaemia Mukt Bharat program.
precautions: Vitamin C rich foods to enhance absorption

guidance: Treatment: Vitamin D (Stoss therapy or daily doses) and calcium supplements. Ensure 15-30 min of sunlight exposure daily. Dietary sources: fortified milk, egg yolk, fish. Government programs provide free Vitamin D supplements.
precautions: Vitamin D supplementation for breastfed infants

guidance: Treatment: lifestyle modification — balanced diet, reduced screen time, 1 hour of physical activity daily. Family-based intervention is most effective. Screen for comorbidities (hypertension, diabetes, fatty liver). Prevention is key.
precautions: Limit sugary drinks and processed food

guidance: Identify and remove source of lead (old paint, contaminated soil, lead pipes, traditional cosmetics). Chelation therapy for severe cases (BAL, EDTA, succimer). Prevention: avoid lead exposure, use lead-free paint, and check for lead in water.
precautions: Do not use traditional cosmetics (kohl, sindoor) with lead

symptoms: dental: white/ brown stains, mottled enamel, pitting
skeletal: joint stiffness, bone pain, curvature of spine, crippling deformities
guidance: Prevent by using safe drinking water (low fluoride). For dental fluorosis: cosmetic dental treatments. For skeletal: orthopedic management, reduce fluoride intake, and ensure good calcium and vitamin D intake.
precautions: If high fluoride, install defluoridation plants
Avoid fluoride toothpaste in young children (until they can spit)
Monitor fluoride levels in drinking water

symptoms: puffiness of face, eyelids, and feet (edema)
recent history of sore throat or skin infection (2-3 weeks prior)
guidance: Treatment: supportive care — fluid and sodium restriction, antihypertensives, diuretics, and antibiotics (penicillin) to clear streptococcal infection. Usually resolves completely in children. Regular blood pressure monitoring.
precautions: Prompt treatment of strep throat and impetigo

symptoms: massive edema (swelling of eyelids, feet, abdomen)
guidance: First-line treatment: oral corticosteroids (prednisolone) for 12 weeks (tapering). Most children respond (steroid-sensitive). Frequent relapses need second-line drugs (levamisole, cyclophosphamide, calcineurin inhibitors). Long-term monitoring for complications (infections, thrombosis).
precautions: Steroid side effects (monitor weight, BP, bone health)

guidance: Diagnosis: urine culture. Treatment: oral antibiotics (cotrimoxazole, amoxicillin, cefalexin) for 7-10 days. Infants < 3 months require IV antibiotics and hospitalization. Investigate for VUR if recurrent UTI or febrile UTI.
precautions: Renal and bladder ultrasound after first febrile UTI

guidance: Diagnosis: VCUG (voiding cystourethrogram). Treatment: low-grade VUR may resolve spontaneously; prophylactic antibiotics reduce UTIs. High-grade VUR or breakthrough infections need surgical correction (ureteral reimplantation or endoscopic injection).

symptoms: delayed motor milestones (not sitting by 9 months, not walking by 18 months)
guidance: Management is multidisciplinary: physiotherapy (Bobath, Vojta), occupational therapy, speech therapy, orthotics, and medications (antispasticity). Early intervention improves outcomes. Free rehabilitation available under RPWD Act 2016 and RBSK. Apply for disability certificate.
precautions: Start therapy as early as possible
Scoliosis and hip dislocation need surgical evaluation

symptoms: no babbling or pointing by 12 months
loss of language or social skills
hyper- or hyposensitivity to sensory inputs
guidance: Early diagnosis is key. Behavioral interventions (ABA — Applied Behavior Analysis), speech therapy, occupational therapy, and social skills training. Parent training is crucial. Children with ASD can learn and thrive with appropriate support. Government: RBSK provides screening, District Early Intervention Centers offer therapy.
precautions: Vaccines do NOT cause autism — continue immunization

symptoms: inattention: difficulty focusing, easily distracted, forgetful
hyperactivity: fidgeting, cannot sit still, running/climbing excessively
impulsivity: interrupts others, acting without thinking
guidance: Diagnosis: comprehensive assessment by a psychiatrist or pediatrician. Treatment: behavioral therapy, parent training, school accommodations, and medications (methylphenidate) if severe. ADHD is not caused by bad parenting or sugar.

symptoms: difficulty with daily living skills (dressing, eating, communication)
guidance: Diagnosis: psychological testing. Management: special education, life skills training, vocational training. Under RPWD Act 2016, free education and rehabilitation services are provided. Apply for disability certificate.
precautions: Plan for adult life (sheltered workshops, group homes)

symptoms: difficulty reading (dyslexia): slow reading, confusion with similar letters (b/d, p/q), skipping words
difficulty with math (dyscalculia): understanding numbers, memorizing tables
difficulty writing (dysgraphia): poor handwriting, spelling errors
guidance: Diagnosis: educational psychologist assessment. Remedial education: multi-sensory teaching, extra time in exams, use of assistive technology. Under RTE Act, children with SLD have the right to reasonable accommodations in school.

Evaluate hearing first. Speech therapy is the mainstay. Encourage language-rich environment — talk, read, and sing to the child. Most cases improve with early intervention. Screen for autism and intellectual disability.

symptoms: delay in two or more developmental domains (gross motor, fine motor, speech, cognitive, social)
guidance: GDD is diagnosed before age 5. Investigation: hearing/vision tests, genetic tests, thyroid, metabolic screening, MRI brain, EEG. Early intervention (physio, speech, occupational) is crucial. Under RBSK, free comprehensive evaluation and therapy are available.
precautions: Apply for disability benefits if permanent

symptoms: types: generalized tonic-clonic (jerking), absence (staring spells), focal (jerking of one limb, confusion)
guidance: Antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) — sodium valproate, carbamazepine, levetiracetam. Medication is FREE at government hospitals. Most children outgrow epilepsy. Avoid triggers: fever, sleep deprivation, photic stimuli. Seizure safety: no unsupervised baths or swimming.
precautions: Seizure first aid (side lying, do not put anything in mouth)

symptoms: generalized jerking of arms and legs
guidance: Simple febrile seizures: self-limiting, no long-term complications. Lay child on side, do not put anything in mouth. Control fever with paracetamol. If seizure lasts > 5 minutes, call 108 (status epilepticus). A single short seizure does not require AEDs.
precautions: Do not put fingers or objects in mouth
Vaccination does not cause febrile seizures

symptoms: child cries vigorously then stops breathing
occurs in children 6 months to 5 years
provoked by anger, fear, or pain
guidance: These spells are frightening but benign — the child always recovers. Do not overreact or punish. Stay calm. If prolonged, perform CPR if needed. Most children outgrow by 5-6 years. No medication needed.
precautions: Do not shake or slap child
Rule out seizures or arrhythmias if atypical

symptoms: signs of liver dysfunction (jaundice, elevated ammonia)
guidance: Reye syndrome is associated with aspirin use in children with viral infections. NEVER give aspirin to children under 18 with fever or viral illness. Prevention: use paracetamol or ibuprofen. Treatment is supportive in ICU.
precautions: Monitor for vomiting and altered consciousness

symptoms: later: peeling of skin on fingers and toes
guidance: Kawasaki disease is a vasculitis — timely treatment with IVIG (intravenous immunoglobulin) and aspirin prevents coronary artery aneurysms. If untreated, risk of heart attack. Early diagnosis is crucial. Echocardiography must be done.
precautions: Seek care for unexplained prolonged fever

symptoms: palpable purpura (rash) on buttocks, legs, and arms
guidance: HSP is self-limiting in most children. Treatment: supportive — hydration, pain relief, steroids for severe abdominal or renal involvement. Monitor urine protein and BP for months to detect nephritis.
precautions: Monitor urine for protein and blood

guidance: Refer to pediatric rheumatologist. NSAIDs, DMARDs (methotrexate), and biologics. Uveitis requires slit-lamp examination. Monitor for eye involvement regularly. Early treatment prevents joint destruction.

symptoms: history of sore throat 2-4 weeks prior
guidance: Diagnosis: Jones criteria. Treat with aspirin or steroids, penicillin to eradicate strep. Prevention of recurrence: regular benzathine penicillin injections (secondary prophylaxis) until age 20. Untreated, it progresses to rheumatic heart disease — a major cause of morbidity in India.
precautions: Dental hygiene to prevent infective endocarditis

symptoms: weight loss or failure to thrive
guidance: Diagnosis: tuberculin skin test (Mantoux), IGRA, chest X-ray, GeneXpert (preferred). Treatment: 6-month DOTS regimen (2HRZE + 4HR). Free under RNTCP. All household contacts should be screened. TB in children is curable.

symptoms: triggered by viral infections, cold air, allergens, exercise
guidance: Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) are the mainstay. Use a spacer with the MDI. Rescue bronchodilator (salbutamol) for acute attacks. Asthma action plan — written by doctor. Identify and avoid triggers. Asthma is manageable.
precautions: Use spacer with inhalers for better delivery
Do not stop controller medications without advice

guidance: Avoid allergens (dust mites, pollen, pet dander). Intranasal corticosteroids and antihistamines. Saline nasal rinses. If severe, allergy testing (skin prick) and immunotherapy.

symptoms: dry, itchy, red patches on skin (face, neck, flexures)
guidance: Moisturizers (emollients) are key — apply frequently. Topical steroids for flares. Avoid triggers (harsh soaps, perfumes, allergens). Identify food triggers in infants (cow's milk, egg).
precautions: Apply moisturizer within 3 minutes of bath

symptoms: usually on face, hands, or feet
guidance: Topical antibiotics (mupirocin) for localized, oral antibiotics (cephalexin) for extensive. Wash lesions with warm water. Prevent spread: avoid sharing towels, good hand hygiene.

symptoms: skin may be tight and shiny
guidance: Oral or IV antibiotics (cephalexin, amoxicillin-clavulanate). Hospitalization for infants or severe cases. Elevate the affected limb. Monitor for abscess or sepsis.
precautions: Seek care if fever or worsening

guidance: IV antibiotics (anti-staphylococcal) as per culture. Surgical drainage for abscess. CRP and ESR for monitoring. Prompt treatment prevents bone necrosis. Common in long bones (femur, tibia).
Emergent condition requiring arthrocentesis and IV antibiotics. Hip joint is most critical (avascular necrosis risk). Surgical washout may be needed. Prevent joint destruction.

symptoms: abdominal pain starting around the umbilicus, migrating to the right lower quadrant
guidance: Surgical emergency — appendectomy. Diagnosis: ultrasound or CT. Perforated appendicitis is common in young children. Do not give analgesics before surgical evaluation.
precautions: Seek care for persistent abdominal pain
Do not give pain relief before evaluation

guidance: Deworming with albendazole (single dose) every 6 months under National Deworming Day. Good hygiene, handwashing, safe water. Iron and nutritional support for anemia.

symptoms: visible white worms in stool or near anus
guidance: Treat the whole family with mebendazole or albendazole (2 doses 2 weeks apart). Maintain strict hygiene: daily bathing, frequent handwashing, daily change of underwear, and washing bedding.

symptoms: visible nits (eggs) attached to hair shafts
guidance: Permethrin 1% lotion or pyrethrin shampoo — apply to scalp, leave for 10 minutes, rinse, comb with a fine-toothed comb. Repeat in 7-10 days. Wash all bedding, hats, and brushes in hot water.
precautions: Do not share combs, hats, scarves

guidance: Oral antifungal therapy is required (griseofulvin or terbinafine) for 6-12 weeks. Topical antifungals alone are ineffective for scalp. Do not use steroid creams (worsens fungal growth).

symptoms: vesicular lesions in the back of the mouth (uvula, tonsils)
guidance: Supportive care — paracetamol for fever, cold fluids, and soft foods. Mouth ulcer gels for pain. It is caused by Coxsackie virus. Resolves in 3-5 days.

Viral: self-limiting, no antibiotics. Bacterial: antibiotic eye drops (chloramphenicol). Allergic: antihistamine drops. Good hygiene is key — highly contagious. Wash hands frequently and avoid touching eyes.

symptoms: ear pain, pulling at the ear
guidance: Amoxicillin is first-line for bacterial. Analgesics for pain. Watchful waiting for mild (48 hours) in older children. Recurrent episodes may need ENT evaluation and possible myringotomy tubes.
Amoxicillin for 10-14 days. Saline nasal rinses, decongestants, and hydration. Persistent cases need CT scan and ENT consultation.

symptoms: red and swollen tonsils with or without exudate (white patches)
guidance: Most are viral (no antibiotics). Bacterial (Group A strep) needs penicillin/amoxicillin for 10 days to prevent rheumatic fever. Rapid strep test or throat culture is recommended.
precautions: Seek care for respiratory distress or trismus

symptoms: rash: fine red bumps (sandpaper-like) on chest, abdomen, flexures
flushed face with pale area around the mouth
peeling skin on hands and feet in later stages
guidance: Group A Streptococcus infection. Treat with penicillin/amoxicillin for 10 days. Good hand hygiene. Complications: acute glomerulonephritis, rheumatic fever if untreated.

symptoms: involuntary urination during sleep in a child over 5 years
at least 2 times per week for 3 months
may be primary (never dry) or secondary (after 6 months of dryness)
guidance: Rule out UTI, constipation, or diabetes. Behavioral: reward for dry nights, limiting fluids in evening, waking to void. Alarm therapy is effective. Desmopressin for short-term use. Most resolve with age.

Increase dietary fiber (fruits, vegetables, whole grains), adequate water intake, and physical activity. If impaction: PEG 4000 (polyethylene glycol) or lactulose is safe. Toilet training schedule (after meals).

symptoms: involuntary passage of stool in inappropriate places (often liquid soiling) in a child > 4 years
associated with chronic constipation and overflow incontinence
guidance: First, treat the underlying constipation with stool softeners. Toilet training and positive reinforcement. Avoid punishment. Often resolves once constipation is managed. Family counseling may help.

symptoms: persistent eating of non-nutritive substances (dirt, chalk, paper, paint, ice) for at least 1 month
may be associated with iron or zinc deficiency
may lead to lead poisoning or bowel obstruction
guidance: Check and treat iron and zinc deficiency. Behavioral interventions. Childproof the home to remove harmful substances. Lead screening is important. Provide alternative sensory stimulation.
precautions: Store harmful substances out of reach

symptoms: eyes appear to point in different directions
guidance: Early evaluation by an ophthalmologist. Patching the good eye (amblyopia treatment), glasses, and eye exercises. Surgery may be needed if not improved by glasses. Early treatment (< 6 years) prevents amblyopia.

symptoms: reduced vision in one eye not correctable by glasses
guidance: Treatment: optical correction (glasses), patching of the good eye (2-6 hours/day), atropine drops to blur the good eye. Best response before age 7-8. Vision screening in schools is essential.
precautions: Amblyopia is preventable if detected early

symptoms: white spots or brown cavities on teeth
guidance: Prevention: brushing with fluoride toothpaste twice a day, avoid night-time bottle-feeding, limit sugary snacks and juices. Dental treatment: fillings, crowns, or extractions. Early dental visit by age 1.

symptoms: hemolytic anemia after exposure to triggers (fava beans, certain drugs, infections)
guidance: Avoid triggers: fava beans, certain drugs (sulfonamides, aspirin, nitrofurantoin, primaquine, dapsone), mothballs (naphthalene). In acute hemolysis, supportive care (blood transfusion). Screening at birth in high-prevalence populations.
precautions: Inform all healthcare providers of G6PD status

symptoms: severe anemia presenting in early infancy (3-6 months)
pale skin, poor feeding, growth retardation
guidance: Lifelong regular blood transfusions (every 3-4 weeks) and chelation therapy (deferasirox, deferoxamine) to prevent iron overload. Bone marrow transplant is the only cure. Prevention: screening of couples (thalassemia carrier detection) and prenatal diagnosis.
precautions: Iron chelation is critical to prevent organ damage

symptoms: sickle cell crises (severe pain in bones, chest, abdomen)
splenic sequestration (sudden enlargement of spleen, shock)
acute chest syndrome (fever, chest pain, respiratory distress)
guidance: Treatment: hydration, pain management, hydroxyurea reduces crisis frequency. Penicillin prophylaxis until age 5 to prevent sepsis. Pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccines. Crisis management at hospital. Newborn screening and comprehensive care.

Diagnosis: growth hormone stimulation test, IGF-1 levels, bone age X-ray, MRI brain (pituitary). Treatment: daily growth hormone injections (available free under some state programs). Good response if started early.
precautions: Regular monitoring of height and IGF-1

guidance: GnRH analog therapy can pause puberty to allow for normal height. Underlying causes (tumor, infection) need evaluation. Psychological support. Refer to pediatric endocrinologist.

Most cases are constitutional delay (family history). Evaluate: bone age, gonadotropins, testosterone/estradiol. Treat underlying cause (hypogonadism, Kallmann syndrome, chronic disease). Hormonal replacement may be indicated.
SURGICAL EMERGENCY. Upper GI contrast study. Emergency surgery (Ladd's procedure). Time to diagnosis is critical for bowel survival. Do not feed.

symptoms: coughing and choking with first feed
guidance: Suspected prenatally or at birth. Confirm with X-ray (NG tube coiled). Surgical repair is the only treatment. Avoid oral feeding until repaired. Good outcomes with early surgery.

symptoms: shift of heart sounds to the right
guidance: Prenatal diagnosis is possible. At birth: immediate intubation, NG tube to decompress stomach. ECMO for severe cases. Surgical repair of the defect. Survival is 70-80% in high-volume centers.
precautions: Long-term follow-up for pulmonary hypertension and reflux

symptoms: unexplained death of an infant < 1 year
guidance: Back to sleep: place baby on the back for every sleep. Avoid soft bedding, pillows, toys, and bumper pads in the crib. Share a room (not bed) for first 6 months. Breastfeeding reduces risk. Avoid overheating.

Lifelong insulin therapy (basal-bolus or insulin pump). Blood glucose monitoring 4-6 times daily. HbA1c every 3 months. Education on hypoglycemia and sick-day rules. Free insulin at government hospitals.
Medical emergency. IV fluids, electrolyte correction. Strict gluten-free diet. Hospitalization for stabilization. Recovery is excellent with treatment.

Measure BP annually in children > 3 years (or earlier if high-risk). Investigate cause: renal, vascular, endocrine. Treatment: lifestyle (diet, exercise), antihypertensives (ACE inhibitors, calcium blockers).

symptoms: family history of premature heart disease
guidance: Screen if family history of hyperlipidemia or early heart disease. Lifestyle: healthy diet, exercise. Statins for children > 8 years with LDL > 160 mg/dL and family history.
Most common cause: adenotonsillar hypertrophy. Refer to ENT for tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy. Weight loss if obese. CPAP for persistent or non-surgical candidates.
